claim: Inferring the causes of illness is a culturally universal example of causal thinking.
source: Inferring the causes of illness is a culturally universal example of causal thinking.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established knowledge about human cognition across cultures.

claim: Making causal inferences about biological processes (e.g. illness) depends on the animacy semantic network.
source: We tested the hypothesis that making causal inferences about biological processes (e.g. illness) depends on the animacy semantic network.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis being tested in the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Participants (n=20) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences across sentences.
source: Participants (n=20) undergoing fMRI read two-sentence vignettes that elicited implicit causal inferences across sentences, either about the emergence of illness or about the mechanical breakdown of inanimate objects, in addition to noncausal control vignettes.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure directly performed in the study.

claim: All vignettes were about people and were linguistically matched.
source: All vignettes were about people and were linguistically matched.
evidence: This describes a key design feature of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Inferring illness causes selectively engaged a portion of the precuneus (PC) previously implicated in the semantic representation of animates.
source: Inferring illness causes, relative to all control conditions, selectively engaged a portion of the precuneus (PC) previously implicated in the semantic representation of animates (e.g. people, animals).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis, supported by both univariate and multivariate analyses.

claim: Neural responses to causal inferences about illness were adjacent to but distinct from responses to mental state inferences.
source: Neural responses to causal inferences about illness were adjacent to but distinct from responses to mental state inferences, suggesting a neural mind/body distinction.
evidence: This finding is supported by the spatial analysis of activation peaks and fROI analyses comparing illness and mentalizing responses.

claim: The study failed to find evidence for domain-general responses to causal inference.
source: We failed to find evidence for domain-general responses to causal inference.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the study, based on the absence of predicted patterns in language and logic networks.

claim: Causal inference is supported by content-specific semantic networks that encode causal knowledge.
source: Causal inference is supported by content-specific semantic networks that encode causal knowledge.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the pattern of results across all analyses.

claim: A distinguishing feature of human cognition is our ability to reason about complex cause-effect relationships, particularly when causes are not directly perceptible.
source: A distinguishing feature of human cognition is our ability to reason about complex cause-effect relationships, particularly when causes are not directly perceptible (Tooby and DeVore, 1987; Lagnado et al., 2007; Rottman et al., 2011; Muentener and Schulz, 2014; Sloman and Lagnado, 2015; Goddu and Gopnik, 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on causal reasoning.

claim: Adults have rich, culturally specific causal knowledge about the invisible forces that bring about illness.
source: Adults have rich, culturally specific causal knowledge about the invisible forces that bring about illness, from pathogen transmission to divine retribution (Notaro et al., 2001; Raman and Winer, 2004; Lynch and Medin, 2006; Legare and Gelman, 2008; Legare et al., 2012; Legare and Shtulman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on cultural variations in illness reasoning.

claim: Even young children think about illness in systematic ways, reflecting their burgeoning commonsense understanding of the biological world.
source: Even young children think about illness in systematic ways, reflecting their burgeoning commonsense understanding of the biological world (Wellman and Gelman, 1992; Keil, 1992; Inagaki and Hatano, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental psychology research.

claim: Young children attribute illness to contaminated food, contact with a sick person, and parental inheritance.
source: Young children attribute illness to contaminated food, contact with a sick person, and parental inheritance (Springer and Ruckel, 1992; Kalish, 1996; Kalish, 1997; Keil et al., 1999; Notaro et al., 2001; Raman and Winer, 2004; Raman and Gelman, 2005; Legare and Gelman, 2008; Legare et al., 2009; DeJesus et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to developmental research on children's illness concepts.

claim: Thinking about living things (animates) as opposed to nonliving things (inanimate objects/places) recruits partially distinct neural systems.
source: Thinking about living things (animates) as opposed to nonliving things (inanimate objects/places) recruits partially distinct neural systems (e.g. Warrington and Shallice, 1984; Hillis and Caramazza, 1991; Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Farah and Rabinowitz, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to classic neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies.

claim: The precuneus (PC) is part of the 'animacy semantic network' and responds preferentially to living things (i.e. people and animals), whether presented as images or words.
source: The precuneus (PC) is part of the 'animacy semantic network' and responds preferentially to living things (i.e. people and animals), whether presented as images or words (Devlin et al., 2002; Fairhall and Caramazza, 2013a; Fairhall et al., 2014; Peer et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Silson et al., 2019; Rabini et al., 2021; Deen and Freiwald, 2022; Aglinskas and Fairhall, 2023; Hauptman et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to prior neuroimaging research on animacy processing.

claim: Parts of the visual system (e.g. fusiform face area [FFA]) that respond preferentially to animates do so primarily for images.
source: By contrast, parts of the visual system (e.g. fusiform face area [FFA]) that respond preferentially to animates do so primarily for images (Kanwisher et al., 1997; Grill-Spector et al., 2004; Noppeney et al., 2006; Mahon et al., 2009; Konkle and Caramazza, 2013; Connolly et al., 2016; see Bi et al., 2016, for a review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on visual processing of animate entities.

claim: The PC represents causal knowledge relevant to animates.
source: We hypothesized that the PC represents causal knowledge relevant to animates and tested the prediction that it would be activated during causal inferences about illness, which rely on such knowledge (preregistration: https://osf.io/6pnqg).
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study, which was preregistered and tested with experimental data.

claim: Some developmental work suggests that children use the same set of causal principles to think about bodies and minds.
source: Both types of inferences are about animate entities, and some developmental work suggests that children use the same set of causal principles to think about bodies and minds (Carey, 1985; Carey, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental psychology research.

claim: By early childhood, young children have distinct causal knowledge about the body and the mind.
source: Other evidence suggests that by early childhood, young children have distinct causal knowledge about the body and the mind (Springer and Keil, 1991; Callanan and Oakes, 1992; Wellman and Gelman, 1992; Inagaki and Hatano, 1993; Inagaki and Hatano, 2004; Keil, 1994; Hickling and Wellman, 2001; Medin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to developmental research.

claim: Preschoolers are more likely to view illness as a consequence of biological causes, such as contagion, rather than psychological causes, such as malicious intent.
source: For instance, preschoolers are more likely to view illness as a consequence of biological causes, such as contagion, rather than psychological causes, such as malicious intent (Springer and Ruckel, 1992; Raman and Winer, 2004; see also Legare and Gelman, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental research on children's illness concepts.

claim: The 'mentalizing network', including the PC, is engaged when people reason about agents' beliefs.
source: The 'mentalizing network', including the PC, is engaged when people reason about agents' beliefs (Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003; Saxe et al., 2006; Saxe and Powell, 2006; Dodell-Feder et al., 2011; Dufour et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging research on mentalizing.

claim: Children and adults make causal inferences across a wide range of domains and use similar cognitive principles when doing so.
source: Children and adults make causal inferences across a wide range of domains and use similar cognitive principles (e.g. 'screening off') when doing so (e.g. Saxe and Carey, 2006; Tenenbaum et al., 2007; Carey, 2011; Cheng and Novick, 1992; Waldmann and Holyoak, 1992; Pearl, 2000; Gopnik et al., 2001; Steyvers et al., 2003; Gopnik et al., 2004; Schulz and Gopnik, 2004; Rehder and Burnett, 2005; Lagnado et al., 2007; Rottman and Hastie, 2014; Davis and Rehder, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to research on causal reasoning across domains.

claim: Prior neuroscience work has hypothesized that the frontotemporal language network may support a broad range of causal inferences during comprehension.
source: Prior neuroscience work has hypothesized that the frontotemporal language network may support a broad range of causal inferences during comprehension (Kuperberg et al., 2006; Mason and Just, 2011; Prat et al., 2011; see also Spelke, 2003; Spelke, 2022; Pinker, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging research on language and causal inference.

claim: Causal inference could depend on frontoparietal mechanisms that also support other types of reasoning, such as logical deduction.
source: Alternatively, causal inference could depend on frontoparietal mechanisms that also support other types of reasoning, such as logical deduction (Goldvarg and Johnson‐Laird, 2001; Barbey and Patterson, 2011; Khemlani et al., 2014; Operskalski and Barbey, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on logical reasoning and its neural basis.

claim: It has been suggested that causal inferences are supported by a dedicated 'causal engine' in prefrontal cortex that supports all and only causal inferences across domains.
source: Finally, it has been suggested that causal inferences are supported by a dedicated 'causal engine' in prefrontal cortex that supports all and only causal inferences across domains (Pramod et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study proposing a domain-general causal inference mechanism.

claim: Most prior studies investigating causal inference used explicit causality judgment tasks.
source: Most prior studies investigating causal inference used explicit causality judgment tasks (Ferstl and von Cramon, 2001; Satpute et al., 2005; Fugelsang and Dunbar, 2005; Kuperberg et al., 2006; Fenker et al., 2010; Kranjec et al., 2012; Pramod et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies of causal inference.

claim: Kuperberg et al., 2006 asked participants to rate the causal relatedness of three-sentence stories and observed higher responses to causally related stories in left frontotemporal cortex.
source: For example, Kuperberg et al., 2006 asked participants to rate the causal relatedness of three-sentence stories and observed higher responses to causally related stories in left frontotemporal cortex.
evidence: This claim describes a specific finding from a cited study.

claim: Studies of implicit causal inference report frontotemporal and frontoparietal responses.
source: Studies of implicit causal inference report frontotemporal and frontoparietal responses (Chow et al., 2008; Mason and Just, 2011; Prat et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Across prior studies, no consistent neural signature of causal inference has emerged.
source: Across these prior studies, no consistent neural signature of causal inference has emerged.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from reviewing the cited literature on causal inference.

claim: In many prior studies, causal trials were more difficult, and/or linguistic variables were not matched across causal and noncausal conditions.
source: Importantly, in many studies, causal trials were more difficult, and/or linguistic variables were not matched across causal and noncausal conditions.
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research methods based on reviewing the literature.

claim: Almost no prior studies localized language or logical reasoning networks in individual participants.
source: In addition, almost no prior studies localized language or logical reasoning networks in individual participants, making it difficult to assess the involvement of these systems (e.g. Fedorenko et al., 2010; Monti et al., 2009; Pramod et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research methods based on reviewing the literature.

claim: Most prior work did not distinguish between causal inferences about different semantic domains known to depend on partially distinct neural networks.
source: Most prior work also did not distinguish between causal inferences about different semantic domains known to depend on partially distinct neural networks, e.g., biological, mechanical, or mental state inferences (cf. Mason and Just, 2011; Pramod et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research methods based on reviewing the literature.

claim: Participants performed a covert task of detecting 'magical' catch trial vignettes that encouraged them to attend to the meaning of the critical vignettes while reading as naturally as possible.
source: Participants performed a covert task of detecting 'magical' catch trial vignettes that encouraged them to attend to the meaning of the critical vignettes while reading as naturally as possible.
evidence: This describes the experimental task design used in the study.

claim: Causal inferences about illness were compared to causal inferences about mechanical breakdown and illness-related language that was not causally connected.
source: Causal inferences about illness were compared to two control conditions: (i) causal inferences about mechanical breakdown (e.g. 'Jake dropped all of his things on the subway. Now he has a shattered phone.') and (ii) illness-related language that was not causally connected (e.g. 'Lynn dropped all of her things on the subway. Now she has a case of COVID.').
evidence: This describes the experimental design and control conditions used in the study.

claim: All vignettes, including mechanical ones, described events involving people.
source: Critically, all vignettes, including mechanical ones, described events involving people, such that responses to causal inferences about illness in the animacy semantic network could not be explained by the presence of animate agents.
evidence: This describes a key design feature of the experimental stimuli to control for confounds.

claim: Noncausal vignettes were constructed by shuffling causes/effects across conditions and were therefore matched to the causal vignettes in linguistic content.
source: Noncausal vignettes were constructed by shuffling causes/effects across conditions and were therefore matched to the causal vignettes in linguistic content.
evidence: This describes the method used to create control stimuli that are linguistically matched.

claim: A separate group of participants rated the causal relatedness of all vignettes prior to the experiment.
source: A separate group of participants rated the causal relatedness of all vignettes prior to the experiment.
evidence: This describes a validation procedure for the experimental stimuli.

claim: The study localized language, logical reasoning, and mentalizing networks in each participant.
source: In addition to the main causal inference experiment, we also localized language, logical reasoning, and mentalizing networks in each participant.
evidence: This describes additional experimental procedures used to identify functional regions of interest.

claim: The primary neural prediction was that animacy-responsive PC would respond more to causal inferences about illness compared to all other control conditions.
source: Following prior work, we predicted that the neural systems that support causal inference would exhibit increased activity during such inferences. Thus, our primary neural prediction was that animacy-responsive PC would respond more to causal inferences about illness compared to all other control conditions.
evidence: This states the main hypothesis of the study, which was tested with fMRI data.

claim: Accuracy on the magic detection task was at ceiling (M=97.9% ± 2.2 SD).
source: Accuracy on the magic detection task was at ceiling (M=97.9% ± 2.2 SD), and there were no significant differences across the four main experimental conditions (Illness-Causal, Mechanical-Causal, Noncausal-Illness First, Noncausal-Mechanical First), F(3,57) = 2.39, p=0.08.
evidence: This reports behavioral results from the experiment.

claim: There were no significant differences in accuracy across the four main experimental conditions.
source: Accuracy on the magic detection task was at ceiling (M=97.9% ± 2.2 SD), and there were no significant differences across the four main experimental conditions (Illness-Causal, Mechanical-Causal, Noncausal-Illness First, Noncausal-Mechanical First), F(3,57) = 2.39, p=0.08.
evidence: This reports behavioral results from the experiment.

claim: A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA evaluating response time revealed a main effect of condition, F(3,57) = 32.63, p<0.001.
source: A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA evaluating response time revealed a main effect of condition, F(3,57) = 32.63, p<0.001, whereby participants were faster on Illness-Causal trials (M=4.73 ± 0.81 SD) compared to Noncausal-Illness First (M=5.33 s±0.85 SD) and Noncausal-Mechanical First (M=5.27 s±0.89 SD) trials.
evidence: This reports behavioral results from the experiment.

claim: Participants were faster on Illness-Causal trials (M=4.73 ± 0.81 SD) compared to Noncausal-Illness First (M=5.33 s±0.85 SD) and Noncausal-Mechanical First (M=5.27 s±0.89 SD) trials.
source: A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA evaluating response time revealed a main effect of condition, F(3,57) = 32.63, p<0.001, whereby participants were faster on Illness-Causal trials (M=4.73 ± 0.81 SD) compared to Noncausal-Illness First (M=5.33 s±0.85 SD) and Noncausal-Mechanical First (M=5.27 s±0.89 SD) trials.
evidence: This reports behavioral results from the experiment.

claim: There were no differences in response time between the Mechanical-Causal condition (M=5.15 s±0.88 SD) and any other conditions.
source: There were no differences in response time between the Mechanical-Causal condition (M=5.15 s±0.88 SD) and any other conditions.
evidence: This reports behavioral results from the experiment.

claim: PC responses during illness inferences overlapped with previously reported responses to people-related concepts.
source: PC responses during illness inferences overlapped with previously reported responses to people-related concepts (Fairhall and Caramazza, 2013b; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This finding is supported by comparison with prior research and visualized in a figure.

claim: Relative to illness inferences and noncausal vignettes, inferring the causes of mechanical breakdown in inanimate entities activated bilateral anterior parahippocampal regions (i.e. anterior PPA).
source: Relative to illness inferences and noncausal vignettes, inferring the causes of mechanical breakdown in inanimate entities activated bilateral anterior parahippocampal regions (i.e. anterior PPA), suggesting a double dissociation between illness and mechanical inferences (Figure 2; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Weiner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fMRI data analysis, supported by statistical tests and visualized in figures.

claim: The anterior PPA region is engaged during memory/verbal tasks about physical spaces.
source: This anterior PPA region is engaged during memory/verbal tasks about physical spaces (Baldassano et al., 2013; Fairhall et al., 2014; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021; Häusler et al., 2022; Hauptman et al., 2025).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the function of anterior PPA.

claim: In individual-subject fROI analysis, inferring illness causes activated the PC more than inferring causes of mechanical breakdown (main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 19.18, p<0.001).
source: In individual-subject functional ROI (fROI) analysis (leave-one-run-out), we similarly found that inferring illness causes activated the PC more than inferring causes of mechanical breakdown (repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Mechanical-Causal) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 19.18, p<0.001, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 0.3, p=0.59, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 27.48, p < 0.001; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The effect of illness inferences on PC activation was larger in the left than in the right PC.
source: This effect was larger in the left than in the right PC (paired samples t-tests; left PC: t(19) = 5.36, p<0.001, right PC: t(19) = 2.27, p=0.04).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: Illness inferences activated the PC more than illness-related language that was not causally connected.
source: Illness inferences also activated the PC more than illness-related language that was not causally connected (repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Noncausal-Illness First) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 4.66, p=0.04, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 2.51, p=0.13, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 8.07, p=0.01; repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Noncausal-Mechanical First) × hemisphere left, right: main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 4.38, p=0.05; main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 1.17, p = 0.29; condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 17.89, p<0.001; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: Increased activity for illness inferences compared to mechanical inferences was observed in the temporoparietal junction (TPJ).
source: We also observed increased activity for illness inferences compared to mechanical inferences in the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) (leave-one-run-out individual-subject fROI analysis; repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Mechanical-Causal) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 5.33, p=0.03, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 1.02, p=0.33, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 4.24, p=0.05; Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The TPJ effect for illness inferences was significant only in the left TPJ.
source: This effect was significant only in the left TPJ (paired samples t-tests; left TPJ: t(19) = 2.64, p=0.02, right TPJ: t(19) = 1.13, p=0.27).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: Unlike the PC, the TPJ did not show a preference for illness inferences compared to illness-related language that was not causally connected.
source: Unlike the PC, the TPJ did not show a preference for illness inferences compared to illness-related language that was not causally connected (repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Noncausal-Illness First) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 0.006, p=0.94, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 2.19, p=0.16, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 1.27, p=0.27; repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Illness-Causal, Noncausal-Mechanical First) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 0.73, p=0.41; main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 1.24, p=0.28; condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 3.34, p=0.08; Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The anterior PPA showed the opposite pattern to PC, responding more to mechanical inferences than illness inferences.
source: In contrast to animacy-responsive PC, the anterior PPA showed the opposite pattern, responding more to mechanical inferences than illness inferences (leave-one-run-out individual-subject fROI analysis; repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Mechanical-Causal, Illness-Causal) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 17.93, p<0.001, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 1.33, p=0.26, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 7.8, p=0.01; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The anterior PPA effect for mechanical inferences was significant only in the left anterior PPA.
source: This effect was significant only in the left anterior PPA (paired samples t-tests; left anterior PPA: t(19) = 4, p<0.001, right anterior PPA: t(19) = 1.88, p=0.08).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The anterior PPA showed a preference for mechanical inferences compared to mechanical-related language that was not causally connected.
source: The anterior PPA also showed a preference for mechanical inferences compared to mechanical-related language that was not causally connected (repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Mechanical-Causal, Noncausal-Illness First) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 14.81, p=0.001, main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 1.81, p=0.2, condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 7.35, p=0.01; repeated-measures ANOVA, condition (Mechanical-Causal, Noncausal-Mechanical First) × hemisphere (left, right): main effect of condition, F(1,19) = 11.31, p=0.003; main effect of hemisphere, F(1,19) = 3.34, p=0.08; condition × hemisphere interaction, F(1,19) = 4, p=0.06; Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: Illness inferences and mechanical causal inferences elicit distinctly localized neural responses.
source: In summary, we found distinctly localized responses to illness and mechanical causal inferences. Inferring illness causes preferentially recruited the animacy semantic network, particularly the PC.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the pattern of fMRI results.

claim: Illness inferences and mental state inferences elicited spatially dissociable responses.
source: Illness inferences and mental state inferences elicited spatially dissociable responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing the spatial patterns of activation for different inference types.

claim: In whole-cortex analysis, illness inferences recruited the PC bilaterally, with larger responses observed in the left hemisphere.
source: In whole-cortex analysis, illness inferences recruited the PC bilaterally, with larger responses observed in the left hemisphere (Figure 1, see also fROI analysis showing left-lateralization above).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-cortex analysis, supported by statistical tests and visualized in figures.

claim: Mental state inferences recruited a broader network, including bilateral PC, bilateral TPJ, superior temporal sulcus, and medial and superior prefrontal cortex.
source: By contrast, and in accordance with prior work (e.g. Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003), mental state inferences recruited a broader network, including not only bilateral PC, but also bilateral TPJ, superior temporal sulcus, and medial and superior prefrontal cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-cortex analysis, consistent with prior research on mentalizing.

claim: Within the left PC, responses to illness inferences were located ventrally to mental state inference responses.
source: Within the left PC, responses to illness inferences were located ventrally to mental state inference responses (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of activation peaks, visualized in figures.

claim: The z-coordinates of individual-subject activation peaks for illness inferences and mental state inferences were significantly different (F(1,19) = 13.52, p=0.002).
source: The z-coordinates of individual-subject activation peaks for illness inferences and mental state inferences were significantly different (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,19) = 13.52, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial analysis of activation peaks, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The size of the illness inference effect was larger in illness-responsive vertices than in mentalizing-responsive vertices in the left PC.
source: In addition, the size of the illness inference effect (Illness-Causal >Mechanical-Causal) was larger in illness-responsive vertices (leave-one-run-out individual-subject fROI analysis) than in mentalizing-responsive vertices in the left PC (individual-subject fROI analysis; repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,19) = 24.72, p<0.001, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis, supported by statistical tests.

claim: Illness inferences and mental state inferences are carried out by neighboring but partially distinct subsets of the PC.
source: These results suggest that illness inferences and mental state inferences are carried out by neighboring but partially distinct subsets of the PC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial and functional dissociation observed in the PC.

claim: Neither the language nor the logic network exhibited elevated neural responses during causal inferences relative to linguistically matched sentence pairs that were not causally connected.
source: In the current study, neither the language nor the logic network exhibited elevated neural responses during causal inferences relative to linguistically matched sentence pairs that were not causally connected.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the fROI analysis of language and logic networks.

claim: Language regions in frontotemporal cortex responded more to noncausal than causal vignettes.
source: Language regions in frontotemporal cortex responded more to noncausal than causal vignettes (frontal search space: repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,19) = 23.91, p<0.001; temporal search space: repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,19) = 4.31, p=0.05; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis of the language network, supported by statistical tests.

claim: The logic network responded marginally more to noncausal vignettes, likely reflecting greater difficulty associated with integrating unrelated sentences.
source: The logic network likewise responded marginally more to noncausal vignettes, likely reflecting greater difficulty associated with integrating unrelated sentences (repeated-measures ANOVA, F(1,19) = 3.88, p=0.07; Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis of the logic network, supported by statistical tests and interpretation.

claim: In whole-cortex univariate analysis, no shared regions responded more to causal than noncausal vignettes across domains.
source: In whole-cortex univariate analysis, no shared regions responded more to causal than noncausal vignettes across domains.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-cortex analysis.

claim: Two whole-cortex univariate contrasts comparing causal and noncausal conditions revealed increased activity for the noncausal condition in bilateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Two whole-cortex univariate contrasts comparing causal and noncausal conditions (Illness-Causal>Noncausal-Mechanical First, Mechanical-Causal>Noncausal-Mechanical First) revealed increased activity for the noncausal condition in bilateral prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-cortex analysis.

claim: The same prefrontal areas that responded more to noncausal than causal stimuli also responded more when participants were slower to complete the task.
source: The same prefrontal areas that responded more to noncausal than causal stimuli also responded more when participants were slower to complete the task, suggesting that these responses reflect a nonspecific difficulty effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole-cortex analysis that includes response time as a covariate.

claim: None of the predicted networks nor any regions across the whole cortex exhibited the predicted domain-general causal inference pattern.
source: In summary, none of the predicted networks nor any regions across the whole cortex exhibited the predicted domain-general causal inference pattern, i.e., larger responses to all causal than all noncausal vignettes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the pattern of fMRI results.

claim: Implicit causal inferences do not depend on domain-general neural mechanisms.
source: These results suggest that implicit causal inferences, which draw upon a person's existing knowledge of relevant causes and effects, do not depend on domain-general neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the absence of domain-general responses in the data.

claim: In searchlight MVPA, illness inferences and mechanical inferences produced spatially distinguishable neural patterns in the left PC extending dorsally into the superior parietal lobule, as well as in left anterior PPA and lateral occipitotemporal cortex.
source: In searchlight MVPA performed across the whole cortex, illness inferences and mechanical inferences produced spatially distinguishable neural patterns in the left PC extending dorsally into the superior parietal lobule, as well as in left anterior PPA and lateral occipitotemporal cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariate pattern analysis.

claim: A whole-cortex searchlight analysis found no shared regions that exhibited significant decoding across all causal vs. noncausal comparisons.
source: A whole-cortex searchlight analysis that tested whether each causal condition could be decoded from each noncausal condition found no shared regions that exhibited significant decoding across all causal vs. noncausal comparisons (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariate pattern analysis.

claim: In individual-subject fROI decoding analyses, illness inferences and mechanical inferences produced spatially distinguishable neural patterns in the left PC, right PC, and left TPJ, as well as in language and logic networks.
source: In individual-subject fROI decoding analyses, illness inferences and mechanical inferences produced spatially distinguishable neural patterns in the left PC, right PC, and left TPJ, as well as in language and logic networks (see Figure 1—figure supplement 12, Supplementary file 2 for full results).
evidence: This is a finding from the multivariate pattern analysis in fROIs.

claim: A semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, particularly the PC, is preferentially engaged when people infer causes of illness compared to when they infer causes of mechanical breakdown or read causally unconnected sentences containing illness-related language.
source: We find that a semantic network previously implicated in thinking about animates, particularly the (PC), is preferentially engaged when people infer causes of illness compared to when they infer causes of mechanical breakdown or read causally unconnected sentences containing illness-related language.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the primary findings.

claim: Mechanical inferences activate an anterior parahippocampal region previously implicated in thinking about and remembering places.
source: By contrast, mechanical inferences activate an anterior parahippocampal region previously implicated in thinking about and remembering places (Baldassano et al., 2013; Fairhall et al., 2014; Silson et al., 2019; Steel et al., 2021; Häusler et al., 2022; Hauptman et al., 2025).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, supported by citations to prior research.

claim: This finding points to a neural double dissociation between biological and mechanical causal knowledge.
source: This finding points to a neural double dissociation between biological and mechanical causal knowledge.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the contrasting patterns of activation for illness and mechanical inferences.

claim: The PC exhibits sensitivity to causal inferences about biological processes specific to animates, such as illness.
source: Here, we show that the PC exhibits sensitivity to causal inferences about biological processes specific to animates, such as illness.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, summarizing the main finding.

claim: Causal knowledge about animate and inanimate entities is distributed across multiple distinct semantic networks.
source: These findings are consistent with our preregistered hypotheses and suggest that causal knowledge about animate and inanimate entities is distributed across multiple distinct semantic networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results showing distinct networks for different types of causal knowledge.

claim: Changes in biological causal knowledge during development, as well as cultural expertise in causal reasoning about illness, influence activity in the animacy network.
source: We hypothesize that changes in biological causal knowledge during development, as well as cultural expertise in causal reasoning about illness (e.g. medical expertise), influence activity in the animacy network (Legare et al., 2012; Norman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis for future research, based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The findings are consistent with prior evidence from naturalistic paradigms showing that the PC is sensitive to discourse-level processes across sentences.
source: Our findings are consistent with prior evidence from naturalistic paradigms showing that the PC is sensitive to discourse-level processes across sentences (e.g. Hasson et al., 2008; Lerner et al., 2011; Lee and Chen, 2022).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to prior research on discourse processing.

claim: PC responses observed during naturalistic narrative comprehension are driven by causal inferences about animate agents.
source: We hypothesize that PC responses observed during naturalistic narrative comprehension are driven by causal inferences about animate agents, who are often the focus of narratives.
evidence: This is a hypothesis for future research, based on the current findings.

claim: PC involvement in episodic memory could be related to animacy-related inferential processes.
source: Likewise, PC involvement in episodic memory could be related to animacy-related inferential processes (DiNicola et al., 2020; Ritchey and Cooper, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis for future research, based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: Neural responses during inferences about biological and mental properties of animates are linked yet separable.
source: We find that neural responses during inferences about biological and mental properties of animates are linked yet separable.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, summarizing the findings on the relationship between illness and mentalizing responses.

claim: Inferring illness causes recruits neural circuits that are adjacent to but distinct from responses to mental state inferences in the PC.
source: Inferring illness causes recruits neural circuits that are adjacent to but distinct from responses to mental state inferences in the PC (Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003; Saxe et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the spatial analysis of activation patterns.

claim: By early childhood, young children provide different causal explanations for biological vs. psychological processes.
source: Even young children provide different causal explanations for biological vs. psychological processes (Springer and Keil, 1991; Callanan and Oakes, 1992; Wellman and Gelman, 1992; Inagaki and Hatano, 1993; Inagaki and Hatano, 2004; Keil, 1994; Hickling and Wellman, 2001; Medin et al., 2010; cf. Carey, 1985; see also Medin and Atran, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental psychology research.

claim: Preschoolers endorse explanations referring to bodily function for why blood flows to different parts of the body, and not to mental states.
source: For example, when asked why blood flows to different parts of the body, 6-year-old endorse explanations referring to bodily function, e.g., 'because it provides energy to the body,' and not to mental states, e.g., 'because we want it to flow' (Inagaki and Hatano, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific developmental study.

claim: Animate entities have a dual nature: they have both bodies and minds.
source: At the same time, animate entities have a dual nature: they have both bodies and minds (Opfer and Gelman, 2011; Spelke, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on concepts of animacy.

claim: The current findings point to the existence of distinct but related neural systems for biological and mentalistic knowledge.
source: The current findings point to the existence of distinct but related neural systems for biological and mentalistic knowledge.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial dissociation between illness and mentalizing responses.

claim: The neuroimaging findings are consistent with evidence from developmental psychology suggesting that causal knowledge is central to human concepts starting early in development.
source: Our neuroimaging findings are consistent with evidence from developmental psychology suggesting that causal knowledge is central to human concepts starting early in development (Keil, 1992; Wellman and Gelman, 1992; Hatano and Inagaki, 1994; Springer and Keil, 1991; Simons and Keil, 1995; Atran, 1998; Keil et al., 1999; Coley et al., 2002; Medin and Atran, 2004).
evidence: This claim connects the current findings to prior developmental research.

claim: According to the 'intuitive theories' account, semantic knowledge is organized into causal frameworks that serve as 'grammars for causal inference'.
source: According to the 'intuitive theories' account, semantic knowledge is organized into causal frameworks that serve as 'grammars for causal inference' (Tenenbaum et al., 2007; Wellman and Gelman, 1992; Gopnik and Meltzoff, 1997; Gopnik and Wellman, 2012; Gerstenberg and Tenenbaum, 2017; see also Boyer, 1995; Barrett et al., 2007; Cosmides and Tooby, 2013; Bender et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work on intuitive theories.

claim: Preschoolers intuit that animates but not inanimate objects get sick and need nourishment to grow and live.
source: For example, preschoolers intuit that animates but not inanimate objects get sick and need nourishment to grow and live (e.g. Rosengren et al., 1991; Kalish, 1996; Gutheil et al., 1998; Raman and Gelman, 2005; see Inagaki and Hatano, 2004; Opfer and Gelman, 2011, for reviews).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental research on biological concepts.

claim: Causal knowledge is encoded in high-level semantic brain networks.
source: The present results suggest that such knowledge is encoded in high-level semantic brain networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that semantic networks are engaged during causal inferences.

claim: The study failed to find sensitivity to causal inference in portions of the ventral stream previously associated with the perception of animate agents.
source: By contrast, we failed to find sensitivity to causal inference in portions of the ventral stream previously associated with the perception of animate agents (see Appendix 4, Figure 1—figure supplement 13 for details).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the study, reported in the appendix.

claim: Sensitivity to causal information may be a distinguishing characteristic of high-level, amodal semantic networks, as opposed to perceptual regions that are activated during semantic tasks.
source: Sensitivity to causal information may be a distinguishing characteristic of high-level, amodal semantic networks, as opposed to perceptual regions that are activated during semantic tasks (e.g. Martin and Chao, 2001; Thompson-Schill, 2003; Barsalou et al., 2003; Binder and Desai, 2011; Bi, 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis drawn from the pattern of results and cited literature.

claim: No brain regions responded more to causal inferences across domains compared to noncausal vignettes in this task.
source: In the current study, participants read two sentence vignettes that either elicited causal inferences or were not causally connected. No brain regions responded more to causal inferences across domains compared to noncausal vignettes in this task.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the whole-cortex analysis.

claim: The language network responded more to noncausal than causal vignettes, possibly due to greater difficulty associated with processing the meaning of a sentence that does not follow from the prior context.
source: The language network responded more to noncausal than causal vignettes, possibly due to greater difficulty associated with processing the meaning of a sentence that does not follow from the prior context.
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis with an interpretation of the result.

claim: Prior studies find that the language network is specialized primarily for sentence-internal processing.
source: Prior studies find that the language network is specialized primarily for sentence-internal processing (Fedorenko and Varley, 2016; Jacoby and Fedorenko, 2020; Blank and Fedorenko, 2020) and patients with agrammatic aphasia can make causal inferences about pictorial stimuli (Varley and Siegal, 2000; Varley, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the language network.

claim: The language system itself is unlikely to support causal inference.
source: Together, these results suggest that the language system itself is unlikely to support causal inference.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and cited literature.

claim: During language comprehension, the language system interacts with semantic networks to enable causal inference.
source: Rather, during language comprehension, the language system interacts with semantic networks to enable causal inference (Simony et al., 2016; Yeshurun et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research on language-semantic interactions.

claim: Responses to causal inference in semantic networks were stronger in the left hemisphere.
source: Notably, in the current study, responses to causal inference in semantic networks were stronger in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a finding from the fROI analysis showing lateralization of effects.

claim: The left lateralization of responses to causal inference may enable efficient interfacing with the language system during comprehension.
source: The left lateralization of such responses may enable efficient interfacing with the language system during comprehension.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of the lateralization finding.

claim: The study failed to find evidence for the claim that the frontoparietal logical reasoning network supports implicit causal inferences.
source: We also failed to find evidence for the claim that the frontoparietal logical reasoning network, a domain-general executive system, supports implicit causal inferences.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the fROI analysis of the logic network.

claim: The study failed to observe elevated responses to causal inference across domains anywhere in the brain in whole-cortex analysis.
source: Finally, we failed to observe elevated responses to causal inference across domains anywhere in the brain in whole-cortex analysis.
evidence: This is a negative finding from the whole-cortex analysis.

claim: The 'reverse causality effect' in prefrontal cortex likely reflects processing demands rather than causal inference per se.
source: A large swath of prefrontal cortex responded more to one noncausal condition (Noncausal-Mechanical First) compared to both causal conditions. The same prefrontal regions also exhibited increased activity when participants were slower to respond to the task. Thus, this 'reverse causality effect' likely reflects processing demands rather than causal inference per se.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prefrontal findings based on the response time covariate analysis.

claim: The elevated prefrontal activity observed for one of the noncausal conditions may reflect the effortful search for a causal connection between sentences when such a connection is difficult to find.
source: An alternative interpretation of the elevated prefrontal activity observed for one of the noncausal conditions is that it reflects the effortful search for a causal connection between sentences when such a connection is difficult to find.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the prefrontal findings.

claim: Domain-general executive mechanisms become engaged when causal inferences are effortful and explicit.
source: This interpretation would suggest that domain-general executive mechanisms become engaged when causal inferences are effortful and explicit.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about when domain-general systems might be engaged in causal inference.

claim: Semantic systems are engaged when we implicitly infer a known causal relationship.
source: By contrast, semantic systems are engaged when we implicitly infer a known causal relationship.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pattern of results showing semantic network engagement during implicit causal inferences.

claim: Domain-general systems likely play an important role in many causal inferences not tested in the current study.
source: Causal inferences are a highly varied class, and domain-general systems likely play an important role in many causal inferences not tested in the current study.
evidence: This is a caveat about the scope of the current findings.

claim: Illness reasoning performed by medical experts proceeds from effects to causes and can involve searching for potential causes within highly complicated and interconnected causal systems.
source: The vignettes used in the current study stipulate illness causes, allowing participants to reason from causes to effects. By contrast, illness reasoning performed by medical experts proceeds from effects to causes and can involve searching for potential causes within highly complicated and interconnected causal systems (Schmidt et al., 1990; Norman et al., 2009; Meder and Mayrhofer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on medical expertise.

claim: The discovery of novel causal relationships and the identification of complex causes may depend in part on domain-general neural mechanisms.
source: The discovery of novel causal relationships (e.g. 'blicket detectors'; Gopnik et al., 2001) and the identification of complex causes, even in the case of illness, may depend in part on domain-general neural mechanisms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about when domain-general mechanisms might be engaged in causal inference.

claim: Causal knowledge is embedded within high-level semantic systems.
source: The present results suggest, however, that causal knowledge is embedded within high-level semantic systems, and that biological causal knowledge is embedded with a semantic system relevant to animacy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the primary findings.

claim: Biological causal knowledge is embedded within a semantic system relevant to animacy.
source: The present results suggest, however, that causal knowledge is embedded within high-level semantic systems, and that biological causal knowledge is embedded with a semantic system relevant to animacy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the primary findings.

claim: Twenty adults (7 women, 13 men, 25–37 years of age, M=28.7 years±3.2 SD) participated in the study.
source: Twenty adults (7 women, 13 men, 25–37 years of age, M=28.7 years±3.2 SD) participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: Two additional participants were excluded from the final dataset due to excessive head motion (>2 mm) and an image artifact.
source: Two additional participants were excluded from the final dataset due to excessive head motion (>2 mm) and an image artifact.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria applied to the participant sample.

claim: The study was reviewed and approved by the Johns Hopkins Medicine Institutional Review Boards (IRB00270868).
source: The study was reviewed and approved by the Johns Hopkins Medicine Institutional Review Boards (IRB00270868).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Explicit causality judgments collected from a separate group of online participants (n=26) verified that both causal conditions were more causally related than both noncausal conditions, t(25) = 36.97, p<0.001.
source: Explicit causality judgments collected from a separate group of online participants (n=26) verified that both causal conditions Illness-Causal, Mechanical-Causal were more causally related than both noncausal conditions, t(25) = 36.97, p<0.001.
evidence: This describes a validation procedure for the experimental stimuli.

claim: Illness-Causal and Mechanical-Causal items received equally high causality ratings, t(25) = –0.64, p=0.53.
source: In addition, Illness-Causal and Mechanical-Causal items received equally high causality ratings, t(25) = –0.64, p=0.53 (see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This describes a validation procedure for the experimental stimuli.

claim: All conditions were matched on multiple linguistic variables known to modulate neural activity in language regions.
source: All conditions were also matched (pairwise t-tests, all ps>0.3, no statistical correction) on multiple linguistic variables known to modulate neural activity in language regions (e.g. Pallier et al., 2011; Shain et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a key design feature of the experimental stimuli to control for linguistic confounds.
